column4: The man who passes a ruined town is made dead for a hundred years and then raised; his question about life after ruin makes vanished life a divinely reversible interval.
Abraham's scattered bird-parts are called and come swiftly, a concrete scene in which what has been dispersed beyond ordinary sight returns to a summons.
For one whom God leaves astray, no path can be found; the verse joins the source's loss-word to the failure to locate a route.
Those who deny the signs are deaf and mute in darkness, while God may place another on a straight path; obscured perception and the road are explicitly paired.
One group is guided while another deserves error because it takes devils as allies yet thinks itself guided; it sharpens the source's contrast between purposeful travel and confident misdirection.
Whoever takes Satan as patron is led astray and then led toward the punishment of the blaze, a false guide whose course has a ruinous destination.
Human formation from dust, death, and the reviving of dead earth culminate in the raising of those in graves; the buried body is not an untraceable disappearance.
After earthly life people die, naming the entrance into the hidden state that the next ayah will reverse.
After death in 23:15, people are raised on the Day of Resurrection, giving that disappearance a specified future end.
At the gathering, the beings once worshipped are asked whether they led the servants astray or the servants themselves lost the way; false companions and lost direction meet in one judgment scene.
Moses strikes the sea and it parts, making a traversable passage through water where the source contrasts a directing path with engulfing loss.
God saves Moses and all who are with him through the opened sea, stating the successful arrival of the route begun in 26:63.
The remaining pursuers are drowned, so the same water marks the contrary end to the protected passage.
God brings living from dead, revives the earth after its death, and says people will likewise be brought out; earth's apparent finality is a sign of emergence.
Those emerging from graves ask who raised them from their resting place, directly continuing 36:51's visible rush toward the Lord.
A single blast brings them all before God, completing the gathering that prevents any buried person from remaining lost.
The skeptic points to decayed bones and asks who can revive them; this is the bodily version of the source's question about being lost in earth.
The answer is that the original Creator gives the bones life and knows every creation, answering disappearance with complete knowledge and recreation.
Barren earth stirs and grows when water descends; the verse expressly makes its revivification a sign that God gives life to the dead.
One who refuses the caller to God cannot escape in the earth and has no protectors; ignoring a summons is called clear error rather than a way out.
Rain gives life to dead land, and the ayah says that such is the coming forth; what lies inert in earth is linked to resurrection.
The earth splits open and people hurry out; the gathering is declared easy for God, reversing the image of bodies swallowed beyond recovery.
Beside the command to walk the earth in 67:15, the warning that it may swallow people marks the boundary between a made-passable ground and sudden loss within it.
The human asks whether God will gather bones, directly challenging the idea that dispersed remains cannot be recovered.
God is able even to proportion the fingertips, so the answer to the lost-body question is exact re-creation rather than a general promise.
Jesus commands worship of God and calls it a straight path; this repeated formulation gives the source's road a worshipful direction.
Breaking the covenant after its pledges is described as straying from the even way, an explicit moral departure from a route.
God takes people in sleep at night and raises them by day until an appointed term, then they return to Him; disappearance from waking sight is ordered toward return.
The Lord knows best who strays from His way and who is guided, placing even moral loss within the complete knowledge opposed to losing and forgetting.
Moses' staff swallows what the magicians had falsified; the source's swallowed-and-gone image meets a scene in which fabrication physically disappears.
Whomever God guides is guided, while those He leaves astray are the losers; it gives the source's two opposed goings a compressed judgment form.
Jacob's eyes turn white from grief over Joseph's absence, joining a lost son to the source's concern with vision and an unseen traveler.
When Joseph's shirt reaches Jacob, his sight returns, reversing the blindness born from the earlier disappearance.
After the sea emergency of 17:67, the warning shifts to land that may swallow people; neither water nor ground provides a place to vanish beyond divine reach.
Jesus' call to worship God concludes, "this is a straight path," repeating the path as a spoken summons rather than an abstract word.
Moses' staff will swallow what the magicians made, another clear instance of fabricated work being made to disappear through swallowing.
The certain Hour includes God's raising all who are in graves, stating the final result toward which 22:5's body-and-earth signs point.
Moses' staff swallows what the magicians fabricated, repeating the physical disappearance of false making that anticipates false claims vanishing at judgment.
The reviving effects of God's mercy on dead earth are explicitly offered as evidence that He gives life to the dead.
In the Fire, followers say their leaders led them astray; the verse supplies a social form of the source's traveler whose direction was seized by another.
The warning that God can cause the earth to swallow people gives a living, catastrophic counterimage to burial in earth and shows that ground is never beyond His control.
A person's evil action is made fair to him while God guides or lets astray; mistaken sight of one's own course parallels the false confidence of those who think themselves guided.
God chooses and guides toward Himself those who turn back, making the terminus of guidance personal and divine rather than merely directional.
Jesus again commands worship of God and identifies it as a straight path, a repeated speaker-and-route formulation alongside 3:51 and 19:36.
The guilty are in error and a blaze; the compact pairing gives ضلال an eschatological end rather than an indefinite wandering.
Only one cry is needed for the resurrection, denying that hidden dead bodies are too dispersed to be summoned.
After that cry, they are suddenly on the open surface, a sharp transition from concealment to visibility.
The Day when secrets are tested brings hidden things out for examination, a nonlexical parallel to the source's concern with what disappears from sight or memory.
The earth tells its news after bringing out its burdens, giving voice to the ground that had enclosed what was hidden.
What lies in breasts is made manifest after the graves are opened, extending bodily emergence to the disclosure of concealed inner contents.
